title: The Market already Knew: A Pre-registered Falsification of TimesFM-3 on the SPY Implied-volatility Surface
abstract: On the day of its release we subjected TimesFM-3, Google's 330-million-parameter multivariate time-series foundation model, to a pre-registered falsification test on a task it has never seen: forecasting the SPY implied-volatility surface (25∆ put, ATM, 25∆ call at 7/30/60/90-day constant maturities) at one-and five-day horizons-against random walk, AR(1), log-HAR, a 3-factor PCA-VAR, and the market's own forward-variance-implied forecast, under pinball loss on its nine native quantiles, with Diebold-Mariano tests, a 90% Model Confidence Set, and a symmetric Mincer-Zarnowitz recalibration. Four results, in the order the kill ladder met them. First, the foundation models win the econometric contest outright: zero-shot, the four TimesFM configurations are the only members of the 90% MCS at h=1 (pinball ×10 3 23.52-23.61 against 23.81 for log-HAR and 24.84 for the PCA-VAR; DM t =-13.7), the gain is uniform across eleven years, and it survives in the Apache-licensed TimesFM-2.5-to our knowledge the first evaluation of a time-series foundation model on option-implied volatility. Variate attention, the release's headline capability, is worth nothing at one day and is what separates the models at five (46.00 against 46.41 univariate, which drops from the MCS). Second, most of the short-horizon edge is calibration, not information: recalibrated, the h=1 MCS readmits the random walk and AR(1), the margin over persistence shrinking from 2.4% to 0.5%-replicating on implied volatility what Brini (2026) found on realized. why: Pre-registered IV forecast test, foundation model, proper stats, real financial task wins.

title: AI-Q-factors: Bringing Economic Discipline to High-dimensional Asset Pricing
abstract: We introduce an empirical asset pricing model that reconciles the flexibility of machine learning with the economic discipline of Q-theory. Our AI-Q-factor model draws on 39 profitability and investment proxies, imposing that high profitability and low investment imply high expected returns. Rather than concentrating on canonical characteristics, it diversifies across roughly 25 signals and doubles the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the Q-factor model. Value and momentum improve on canonical Q-factors but are redundant against AI-Q-factors, even when measured using refined or high-dimensional characteristics. The AI-Q-factor model thus provides a new benchmark that improves measurement of the factors while maintaining the economic structure of the Q-factor model.
why: Solid ML factor model, OOS validation, but not LLM-focused

title: Extreme Media Sentiment and Stock Price Crash Risk: Evidence from Large Language Models
abstract: This study examines whether the intensity of media sentiment predicts future stock price crash risk (SPCR). Using DistilBERT to classify firm-related financial news into five sentiment categories, we report a pronounced asymmetry: higher future SPCR is associated specifically with extreme positive sentiment, whereas mild positive and negative sentiment show no comparable association. The effect of extreme positive sentiment operates through three distinct behavioral channels: heightened retail investor optimism, greater optimism bias in analyst forecast, and more intensive managerial earnings management. In contrast, negative sentiment primarily induces cautionary responses but has no significant effect on subsequent SPCR. Greater media visibility amplifies the responses of retail investors and firm managers, while prompting a corrective response among professional analysts. Overall, this study shows that the relation between media reporting and SPCR depends on sentiment intensity rather than polarity alone, with extreme optimism emerging as the economically salient dimension of media sentiment in shaping future SPCR. These findings are robust to alternative SPCR measures, sentimentclassification approaches, human validation, alternative specifications, and placebo tests.
why: Real LLM on financial text (news sentiment), real phenomenon, but single market.

title: Evidence-Gated GraphRAG: A Decision-LayerSoundness Framework for Hallucination-ResistantCyber-Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes cyber-financial enviroments, but they continue to hallucinate even under retrievalor knowledge-graph augmentation. We argue this is a decision-control fail-ure rather than a generation defect: existing architectures lack a principledmechanism for refusing to decide under insufficient or contradictory evidence.We introduce EG-GraphRAG, an evidence-gated GraphRAG framework thatmakes abstention a first-class architectural outcome through three components:similarity-thresholded admissibility filtering, Multi-Node Evidence Agreement(MNEA) and a deterministic generation-free decision layer in which the LLMserves only as a post-hoc explainer. We prove a conditional decision-layer sound-ness theorem that decomposes hallucination risk into upstream extraction errorand conditional MNEA survival, and we derive a non-trivial upper bound onthe latter from graph structural properties (Proposition 1). On a 462-transcriptheld-out test set, EG-GraphRAG attains F1 = 0.961 at 85.8% coverage andretains a statistically significant advantage over eleven baselines under matched-coverage and Risk–Coverage-AUC evaluation. title: Benchmark Choice and the Measurement of Institutional Portfolio Convergence: Evidence from SEC Form 13F Holdings and form ADV Disclosures, 2013–2026
abstract: A recent CFA Institute framework paper (Naqvi, 2026) argues that artificial intelligence is producing cognitive convergence in asset management and asserts that each element of the framework "is already observable across today's capital markets" (p. 17). This study evaluates the observable implications of that claim using SEC Form 13F institutional holdings (52 quarters, 2013Q2–2026Q1, of which the final quarter is provisional at the data cut; 2,840 to 7,349 managers per quarter) and Form ADV Part 2A adviser brochures (2019 and 2024). A first estimate reproduces the pattern the claim predicts: measured against the value-weighted market benchmark, mean pairwise similarity of managers' active portfolios rises approximately 330 per cent, and the largest structural-break statistic falls in late 2022. Both results prove highly sensitive to measurement choices. Replacing the market benchmark with the average-manager portfolio changes the estimate from +330 per cent to −7.8 per cent, and an exact stock-level decomposition attributes approximately 86 per cent of the headline increase to the ten largest securities, whose contribution to the measure roughly quadrupled while their share of aggregate value roughly doubled. Under a sup-F test with a parametric bootstrap, the full-sample series shows no significant break (p = 0.109), placebo series constructed from the same panel produce significant breaks at unrelated dates, and the late-2022 break statistic falls from 13.0 to 0.69 when the ten largest stocks are excluded. The break analysis is accordingly treated as exploratory throughout. Three findings are more durable. First, the effective number of statistically distinct portfolios among a fixed panel of 1,302 managers declines in every specification examined: by 51 per cent on raw holdings, by 54 per cent against an average-manager benchmark, and by 25 per cent (35 per cent on four-quarter means) in the strictest specification that both changes the benchmark and excludes the ten largest stocks. Second, within- quarter herding (Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny, 1992) rises 57 per cent, while cross-quarter following (Sias, 2003) falls 19 per cent and median turnover falls 29 per cent, the latter two contrary to the framework's prediction of increasing speed and synchronisation. Third, among the 586 advisers observed in both brochure vintages, the share whose Form ADV Part 2A mentions artificial intelligence rises from 0.85 per cent to 4.10 per cent (exact McNemar test, p = 0.000066); this is a disclosure result, not an adoption estimate, and the study establishes no causal link between AI and any portfolio-level change. The paper additionally reproduces the direction and approximate magnitude of the one published raw- similarity estimate (Meng and Chen, 2026a): applying their $500 million size filter to this panel yields a +16.8 per cent rise in raw cosine similarity over their sample window, against their +12 per cent. The main contribution is methodological: index-relative and manager-relative convergence are distinct quantities, and in this data the choice between them determines the sign of the headline result. The principal limitations are the 2013 start of the structured 13F archive, in-sample validation of the text classifier, and the absence of direct passive-mandate controls.
why: Portfolio convergence real but measurement-sensitive; not actionable.

title: Words vs. Facts：Earnings Call Inconsistency and Stock Price Delay
abstract: This paper examines whether inconsistencies between managers' earnings call narratives and contemporaneous financial fundamentals convey incremental information about market pricing efficiency. Using a sample of firms listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange Sci-Tech Innovation Board (SSE STAR Market) from 2019 to 2023, we construct a Contradiction Index by deploying the DeepSeek large language model with chain-of-thought prompting. This index captures the severity of divergence between managerial claims in Q&A exchanges and realized financial outcomes. We document that greater inconsistency is associated with a significantly lower stock price delay, implying that contradictory signals accelerate the incorporation of firm-specific information into prices. The same index also negatively predicts future profitability and increases analyst forecast dispersion, indicating that divergence between words and facts carries information that extends beyond the tone of managerial language.

title: From Human vs. Human to Algorithm vs. Algorithm: The Asymmetric Effects on Accounting Information Transparency
abstract: This paper examines the asymmetric effects of regulatory technology (RegTech) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the transparency of accounting information. Using a sample of Chinese A-share firms listed between 2015 and 2024, we exploit the staggered implementation of intelligent regulatory platforms by the Shenzhen and Shanghai Stock Exchanges and the widespread adoption of GenAI following the introduction of ChatGPT in 2023. We find that RegTech significantly improves transparency in terms of accounting information in that firms conceal fewer disclosures. Additionally, RegTech provides a strong regulatory deterrent. By contrast, the widespread adoption of GenAI progressively weakens these transparency gains, with more firms evading disclosure and more instances of regulatory misalignment. However, the governance effects do vary with each firm’s internal practices, technological capabilities, and regulatory environments. We further show that greater transparency increases firm value and reduces financing costs. These findings introduce algorithmic capture as a mechanism through which incorporating GenAI into a firm’s way of doing business makes digital regulation more effective. We also provide new evidence on the interactions between RegTech, GenAI, and accounting information transparency.
why: Solid empirical work on GenAI effects, single country, not actionable for trading.

title: Can Sci-Tech Finance Pilot Policy Nurture Patient Capital? Evidence from Double Machine Learning
abstract: This study examines the causal effect of the Sci-Tech Finance Pilot Policy (STFPP) on patient capital among Chinese listed enterprises. Patient capital is disaggregated into strategic equity, proxied by the stability of institutional investor shareholdings, and relational debt, captured by the ratio of long-term liabilities to total liabilities. Leveraging the staggered rollout of the STFPP, we employ a Double Machine Learning framework to estimate policy treatment effects while accommodating nonlinear confounding relationships. Using panel data spanning 2011 to 2023, we find that the STFPP significantly increases both components, with a comparatively stronger effect on strategic equity. Mechanism analyses reveal three transmission channels: alleviating financing constraints, expanding credit financing scale, and prolonging long-term borrowing. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that state-owned enterprises, large-scale firms, and firms with low existing bank debt experience more pronounced gains. These findings suggest that technology finance policies reshape the temporal and governance structure of capital, fostering an ecosystem conducive to sustained innovation.
why: Sound causal inference (DML), but single-country policy context limits generalization.

title: An Equity-Effectiveness Tradeoff in Sectoral Job Training? Evidence from Year Up
abstract: In the context of a randomized evaluation of a prominent sectoral job-training program (named Year Up), we apply machine learning techniques to study both the implications of earnings impact heterogeneity for applicant selection and potential explanations for why program impacts vary across individuals. We document that those in the top predicted impact quintile experience roughly three times the earnings boost relative to those in the bottom impact quintile. Those who benefit least are disproportionately Black, female, poor, and low-skilled, which implies an equity-effectiveness tradeoff. In particular, relative to the max impact cohort, selecting the most "disadvantaged" cohort results in an MVPF loss of approximately 16%. But, despite this, we show suggestive evidence that the program's current selection procedure results in cohorts within the equity-effectiveness frontier, potentially leaving Pareto gains on the table. We conclude by showing that the earnings impact heterogeneity is more strongly associated with predicted impacts on job quality than predicted impacts on soft skills.

title: Predictive Business Analytics for Organizational Risk Management Using Machine Learning
abstract: This study examines how predictive business analytics and machine learning can strengthen organizational risk management in volatile and interconnected business environments. Organizations face financial, operational, technological, cybersecurity, supply-chain, and strategic risks whose interactions can amplify disruption. Traditional enterprise risk management (ERM) remains valuable for identifying and assessing known risks, but periodic assessment and retrospective reporting may provide limited early warning of emerging threats. Predictive business analytics addresses this limitation by using historical and current data to identify patterns, estimate probabilities, and support anticipatory decision-making (Chen et al., 2012; Shmueli & Koppius, 2011). The study adopts a structured integrative literature review and comparative conceptual analysis of research on ERM, business analytics, predictive analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. The synthesis indicates that Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost can support risk classification, anomaly detection, and predictive estimation when matched to appropriate data and decision contexts. The findings further emphasize that predictive performance depends on data quality, model selection, validation, interpretability, governance, and meaningful human oversight. The study contributes an integrated analytical model linking organizational risk data, analytics, machine-learning intelligence, managerial interpretation, governance, and continuous learning. AI-assisted tools were used for language editing and formatting support; the author reviewed and assumes responsibility for the final content.

title: Procedural Knowledge Is Not Redundant: When, Where, and How AI Belongs in the Accounting Curriculum
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now performs many procedural tasks long taught in accounting data analytics courses, raising questions about what constitutes technical competence and when, where, and how AI should be integrated across the accounting curriculum. This commentary argues that procedural knowledge does not become redundant under generative AI; rather, its educational purpose shifts toward enabling students to supervise AI-generated work. Drawing on research on automation, expertise, and human oversight, we propose a Specification–Prediction–Audit (SPA) framework for organizing this supervisory competence. We argue that full engagement with SPA requires foundational technical and domain knowledge and therefore raises an important curricular sequencing and placement question. Using data analytics as a motivating case, we distinguish early diagnostic uses of AI from later, more substantive reliance and propose a capstone integrating multiple accounting domains as a promising venue for developing AI-supervision competence. We conclude with a research agenda for empirically testing these propositions. The commentary reframes the debate over preserving procedural instruction as a testable question of how and where the expertise needed to supervise AI should be developed.
why: Position paper on accounting pedagogy; not implementation-focused.

title: A Double-Auction Market for Compute-Power Coordinated Workload Migration in Geo-Distributed AI Data Centers
abstract: Geo-distributed AI data centers (DCs) provide substantial flexibility for reducing operational costs and carbon emissions through compute-power coordination, which enables workloads to be executed at environmentally favorable locations and times. Existing studies primarily rely on centralized scheduling algorithms that assume cooperative participation among DCs, while resource trading mechanisms focus mainly on the economic benefits of individual participants and less on the broader system-level benefits. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Social Welfare-Aware Resource Market (SWARM), a two-layer market-based compute-power coordination framework that enables resource exchange among autonomous DCs while optimizing overall social welfare. Specifically, the Market Layer employs a continuous double-auction mechanism to incentivize truthful compute-resource trading, while the Welfare Layer coordinates workload migration based on the Market Layer outcomes to maximize external welfare. We theoretically prove that the proposed mechanism provides the necessary economic guarantees for autonomous DC coordination, which include truthful participation, voluntary cooperation, financial feasibility, and efficient resource allocation. Extensive simulations demonstrate that SWARM consistently outperforms representative scheduling and market-based baselines. Compared with the strongest baseline, SWARM reduces operating cost by 49.6%, reduces carbon emissions by 62.9%, increases renewable-energy utilization by 37.6%, and improves social welfare by 13.7%.

title: Artificial Intelligence and International Expansion: How Digital Capabilities Shape the Foreign Market Performance of SMEs
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet the international-business literature has not fully explained why some SMEs convert AI investments into stronger foreign-market outcomes while others do not. This paper develops and tests an integrated dynamic-capabilities model in which AI capability supports foreign-market performance partly by building digital capabilities for market sensing, customer engagement, cross-border coordination, data integration, and rapid process reconfiguration. Foreign-market dynamism is proposed as a boundary condition that increases the value of these capabilities when overseas customer preferences, competitor actions, channel requirements, and regulatory conditions change quickly. To demonstrate a complete empirical design, the manuscript uses an explicitly simulated two-wave dataset calibrated to the characteristics of 342 export-active SMEs. The simulated analysis follows a journal-style protocol including measurement reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, collinearity checks, bootstrapped structural paths, mediation, moderation, predictive assessment, and robustness tests. The illustrative findings show that AI capability is strongly associated with digital capability, that both AI and digital capability contribute to foreign-market performance, and that digital capability partially mediates the AI–performance relationship. The digital capability effect is also stronger under high foreign-market dynamism. The paper contributes by distinguishing AI possession from AI-enabled organizational capability, by positioning digital capability as the conversion mechanism through which AI resources become international competitive outcomes, and by specifying environmental conditions under which this mechanism is particularly valuable. For managers, the model implies that acquiring AI tools is insufficient: SMEs need complementary data routines, employee skills, integration practices, experimentation processes, and market-facing digital workflows. Because the numerical evidence is simulated rather than collected from human respondents, it should be replaced with real field data before any empirical submission or claim of actual findings.Keywords; Artificial intelligence capability; digital capability; SME internationalization; foreign market performance; dynamic capabilities; export performance; market dynamism; international expansion
